title: Portable Trusted Linux
summary: Portable Trusted Linux is a portable security environment designed to boot independently of an installed operating system, authenticate its own trusted components, collect hardware-backed boot evidence where available, run with minimal persistence, produce independently verifiable attestation records, and preserve the history of those records through cryptographic evidence anchoring.

sections.title: Project objective
sections.content:
The project begins with a simple problem: if the operating system already installed on a computer may be compromised, asking that operating system whether the computer is safe creates a circular trust problem.

Portable Trusted Linux therefore aims to boot directly from independently verified USB media without relying on the installed Windows or Linux system. The system builds confidence in stages rather than presenting a simplistic SAFE or UNSAFE answer.

The central design rule is that every conclusion must state what was verified, how it was verified, which trust anchor was used, and what remains unknown or outside the available trust model.

sections.title: Runtime trust chain
sections.content:
The current runtime trust chain is: authenticated signing/release reference -> verified USB image -> UEFI / Secure Boot -> measured boot and TCG event log -> TPM PCR evidence -> signed Unified Kernel Image -> authenticated dm-verity root hash -> immutable Linux root filesystem -> disposable RAM-backed writable state -> nonce-bound TPM Quote -> independent verifier -> attestation report.

No individual stage proves that the entire computer is safe. Each technology is deliberately assigned a narrower claim that can be tested.

sections.title: Cryptographic image verification
sections.content:
Cryptographic hashes such as SHA-256 act as precise digital fingerprints. A matching digest gives very strong evidence that accessible data matches a reference. It does not by itself prove who created that reference or whether the reference is trustworthy.

Authenticity therefore comes from trusted digital signatures or another independently established trust anchor. After writing the Linux image to USB, full media read-back can be hashed again to verify the storage that the computer can actually read.

sections.title: Boot security
sections.content:
Modern PCs generally begin execution in UEFI firmware before Windows or Linux starts. Secure Boot checks whether boot software is authorised under the configured signing policy. Measured Boot is separate: it records cryptographic measurements describing important startup events.

The prototype plans to use a signed Unified Kernel Image where practical so the kernel, initrd and important boot metadata can be bound into a defined signed and measured object.

sections.title: TPM, PCRs and attestation
sections.content:
A TPM 2.0 can provide protected platform-security functions and measurement registers. Platform Configuration Registers accumulate measurements during startup, while the TCG event log supplies evidence describing measured events.

The verifier supplies a fresh random nonce. The target TPM produces a Quote covering selected PCRs and the nonce. The verifier checks the Quote, nonce, PCR selection, event-log consistency where supported, attestation-key policy and the appropriate reference profile.

The target PC is the Attester; it must not be the sole authority deciding whether its own evidence is acceptable.

sections.title: Immutable Linux and dm-verity
sections.content:
The trusted Linux root filesystem should remain read-only during normal operation. dm-verity protects the root at block level using a Merkle tree whose authenticated root hash is bound into the trusted boot path.

Temporary writable state is separated into a RAM-backed overlay. This provides a normal working environment while ensuring ordinary session changes disappear on shutdown unless deliberately exported. RAM-backed operation reduces persistence but is not claimed to defeat all physical or live-memory attacks.

sections.title: Hardware and firmware limits
sections.content:
The project distinguishes software integrity from hardware trust. A matching USB image digest does not prove the USB controller firmware itself is trustworthy. A valid TPM Quote does not automatically prove every firmware component, option ROM, peripheral controller or physical component is uncompromised.

Where trusted reference information exists, measurements can be evaluated. Where evidence is unavailable, the correct states are UNKNOWN or NOT VERIFIABLE rather than an unsupported VERIFIED result.

sections.title: Independent multi-PC corroboration
sections.content:
The same portable image can be tested on multiple independent PCs. Each host can independently reproduce the portable-image identity while producing its own machine-specific TPM, firmware and boot evidence.

This is called independent corroboration, not proof by multiple PCs. PCRs are often host-, firmware-, update- and configuration-specific, so unrelated PCs should not be expected to have identical PCR values. Stable portable-image identity can be compared universally while host evidence is evaluated against host-appropriate reference policy.

sections.title: Evidence-history trust chain
sections.content:
Version 0.2 introduced a second trust chain concerned with the history of evidence. The proposed sequence is: attestation report -> canonical representation -> SHA-256 -> digital signature -> previous-report hash -> local hash chain -> external evidence anchor.

This helps detect retrospective editing or replacement of reports. A complete local compromise could still regenerate a local chain, which is why an independent external commitment is valuable.

sections.title: Transparency logs and blockchain
sections.content:
The core architecture uses the neutral term External Evidence Anchoring. A cryptographic transparency log is the preferred first public backend because the project's need is an auditable append-only security-evidence history rather than a financial transaction system.

A public blockchain may be used as an optional secondary commitment or timestamp layer. Only a cryptographic commitment should normally be published; the full attestation report remains private.

An external ledger proves that a commitment was recorded. It does not prove that the original measurement was true. Measurement quality comes from the earlier verification and attestation chain.

sections.title: Offline-first verification
sections.content:
The initial trust assessment should work without Internet access. The preferred workflow is: boot offline -> authenticate portable OS -> collect platform evidence -> verify immutable root -> create report -> calculate/sign commitment -> store pending anchor -> later enable approved networking -> publish external commitment.

External publication therefore does not become a dependency of trusted boot.

sections.title: Repository and documentation model
sections.content:
Version 0.3 establishes this private GitHub repository as the canonical development workspace. Human-readable documents live under docs/, the canonical public-viewer source lives under web/, and project_content.json is the machine-readable living project index.

Git commits preserve all historical repository states. Documents should normally be extended or superseded by explicit versioned changes rather than silently erasing important earlier decisions. The living JSON should be updated last after substantive project changes so it accurately indexes the repository's current state.

sections.title: Current prototype direction
sections.content:
The current engineering milestone is Prototype Build Specification v0.1. The first implementation remains deliberately small: Debian Live, signed UKI, UEFI Secure Boot where practical, TPM 2.0 measured-boot evidence, dm-verity, RAM-backed disposable state, canonical attestation bundle and an independent command-line verifier.

External evidence anchoring is designed into the report model now, but transparency-log or blockchain publication follows only after the local trust chain and verifier work correctly.

decisions.title: Do not build a new Linux distribution from scratch
decisions.text: Use mature Linux and platform security components and focus custom engineering on verification, evidence and orchestration.

decisions.title: Debian Live selected as the initial base
decisions.text: The first prototype will use Debian Live rather than a custom kernel or operating-system stack.

decisions.title: Separate Secure Boot from Measured Boot
decisions.text: Secure Boot controls authorised execution while Measured Boot records evidence. The architecture uses both where practical rather than treating them as interchangeable.

decisions.title: TPM evidence requires independent verification
decisions.text: The target machine will not turn TPM presence into a self-issued SAFE result. Quotes, PCRs, event logs and reference policy are independently evaluated.

decisions.title: Unknown and Not Verifiable are valid security states
decisions.text: Unsupported or unverifiable components are reported explicitly rather than implicitly treated as trusted.

decisions.title: Add External Evidence Anchoring
decisions.text: Attestation reports will support canonical hashing, signatures, previous-report linkage and later independent publication of cryptographic commitments.

decisions.title: Do not publish full attestation reports to immutable public ledgers
decisions.text: Public anchoring should normally publish only a cryptographic commitment because full reports may contain sensitive platform information.

decisions.title: Transparency log first, blockchain optional
decisions.text: The project uses a backend-neutral External Evidence Anchoring abstraction. A transparency log is preferred initially and public blockchain anchoring remains optional.

decisions.title: Verification remains offline-first
decisions.text: External evidence publication is not a dependency of trusted boot or initial assessment; commitments can be published after approved networking is enabled.

decisions.title: GitHub becomes the canonical development workspace
decisions.text: Project documents, web-viewer source and the living project index are stored in the private portable-trusted-linux repository. Git commits preserve development history.

decisions.title: Update project_content.json last
decisions.text: After repository files or project documents change, the living JSON index is updated as the final repository write so the public project page reflects the complete current state.
